- Labs: blood count (for anemia), electrolytes and kidney function, liver function, thyroid function.
- Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium finds inflammatory, ischemic or infiltrative processes such as sarcoidosis and hemochromatosis.
- Biopsy is not routine and rarely useful. It is done only for recent, rapidly deteriorating function or a systemic disease that can involve the heart (hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis).

cards.t: B-type natriuretic peptide in heart failure
q: what does a low BNP mean
why is BNP elevated in heart failure
what BNP level excludes heart failure
cards.x:
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a blood marker released when the filling pressures inside the ventricles are high. So it is elevated in heart failure. A level below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure an unlikely explanation for the current symptoms.

Think of it as a rule-out test: a low number makes a failing heart an unlikely reason for the symptoms, while a high number fits a heart that is struggling against high filling pressure.

cards.t: Treating dilated cardiomyopathy: drugs
q: how do you treat dilated cardiomyopathy
which drugs lower mortality
when should you anticoagulate in DCM
cards.x:
Treatment is essentially that of chronic heart failure. Every patient, whatever the cause, gets a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

The drug classes:
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (the criterion standard; they lower mortality; for example lisinopril).
- Beta blockers (carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol), which also lower mortality.
- Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan).
- An aldosterone receptor blocker (spironolactone), given with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
- Sacubitril/valsartan.
- Nitrates, for pulmonary edema.
- Diuretics, with loop diuretics the mainstay.
- Antiarrhythmics (amiodarone for supraventricular and nonsustained ventricular tachycardia).

Anticoagulants are used only for atrial fibrillation, an artificial valve or a known mural thrombus (a clot on the heart wall). The dilated ventricle carries clot risk, but these three are the indications.

Education means removing the offending source (alcohol, nutritional deficiency, cardiotoxic agents). It also means restricting sodium to under 2 g a day. Offer genetic counseling when there is a family history.

cards.t: Devices, assist devices, transplant and prognosis in dilated cardiomyopathy
q: when is a defibrillator placed in DCM
what is a left ventricular assist device
what is the prognosis of dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
When drugs are not enough, devices step in.

- A biventricular pacemaker is for moderately severe left ventricular dysfunction.
- An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (a device that shocks a dangerous rhythm) is placed if the ejection fraction is below 35% after maximum medical therapy. A biventricular defibrillator combines the two.
- A left ventricular assist device pumps blood from the left ventricle into the aorta. It can be a bridge to transplantation or to recovery of function, or destination therapy for those who cannot have a transplant. Patients may live more than 5 years with one.
- Cardiac transplantation is the other option, and idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy is its primary indication.

Prognosis is poor overall and depends on the response to therapy. Once symptoms emerge, there is 50% mortality at 5 years, largely from progressive disease and sudden death from an arrhythmia.

cards.t: Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation murmurs in dilated cardiomyopathy
q: where is the mitral regurgitation murmur heard
how do you tell tricuspid from mitral regurgitation
what makes the mitral regurgitation murmur louder
cards.x:
As the dilated heart stretches, the valve apparatus is distorted and the valves leak backward (regurgitation). Mitral regurgitation comes earlier, and tricuspid regurgitation follows. Both murmurs are holosystolic, meaning they fill all of systole, so the way to tell them apart is where they are loudest and where they travel.

- Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic, loudest at the apex, radiating to the left axilla, and louder with handgrip or squatting.
- Tricuspid regurgitation: holosystolic at the lower left sternal border, radiating to the right sternum and xiphoid but not to the axilla, and slightly louder with inspiration.

A simple way to remember it: mitral goes out to the armpit, tricuspid stays near the breastbone and gets louder when the patient breathes in.

cards.t: Acute myocarditis: what it is and what causes it
q: what is myocarditis
what causes myocarditis
who gets myocarditis
cards.x:
Acute myocarditis is inflammation of the myocardium (the heart muscle), ranging from subtle to devastating. It usually strikes an otherwise healthy person and can cause rapidly progressive, often fatal heart failure and arrhythmia. Young males are particularly susceptible, though men and women are affected about equally, with no race predilection.

In developed countries, viral infection is presumed to be the most frequent cause: parvovirus, human herpesvirus 6, enteroviruses (Coxsackie B), adenoviruses, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, and coronavirus disease 2019. Viral myocarditis accounts for 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy.

Other causes:
- Rheumatic fever (beta-hemolytic streptococcus; the heart is affected in 50 to 90%).
- Bacteria such as diphtheria and Legionnaires disease.
- Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas), rickettsia, spirochetes such as Lyme disease, and Candida.
- Drugs (penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline, methyldopa).
- Toxins (lithium, arsenic, lead, copper).
- Autoimmune disease (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis).

cards.t: How acute myocarditis presents
k: new heart failure in a healthy young person
q: what are the symptoms of myocarditis
what is the classic history for viral myocarditis
what is on the differential for myocarditis
cards.x:
The classic story is acute decompensated heart failure in a person with no underlying heart problem or a low cardiac risk. In viral myocarditis there is often a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier (fever, muscle aches, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or stomach upset). A flulike illness that clears and is followed by new heart failure symptoms is the big clue.

Then come exercise intolerance, shortness of breath, fluid retention and chest pain. Palpitations, fainting or sudden cardiac death follow too, caused by ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block.

On exam, the patient may be in cardiogenic shock or frank heart failure: fast heart rate, low blood pressure, raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound, crackles and swelling.

The differential includes tamponade, cardiogenic shock, cocaine cardiomyopathy, ischemic heart disease, valve disease and coronary atherosclerosis. It also includes the dilated, hypertrophic, peripartum and restrictive cardiomyopathies.

cards.t: Diagnosing myocarditis: troponin, magnetic resonance imaging and biopsy
q: what is the gold standard test for myocarditis
what test shows the extent of inflammation
when is a biopsy done for myocarditis
cards.x:
The work-up shows inflammation and heart muscle damage while excluding other causes.

- Blood count: leukocytosis (a raised white cell count). Sedimentation rate: may be raised.
- Troponin: the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis (heart muscle cell death).
- Electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias.
- Echocardiogram, and a chest X-ray that is nonspecific but may show an enlarged heart.
- Cardiac angiography, to rule out coronary ischemia as the cause of new heart failure.
- Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging shows the extent of inflammation.

Endomyocardial biopsy (a sample of heart muscle) is the gold standard, but only once other causes of heart failure are excluded. It is recommended for acute deterioration of unknown origin that is not responding to treatment.

So there is a split: magnetic resonance imaging is the best test to see the extent, while biopsy is the definitive one that is rarely done.

cards.t: Myocarditis: management and prognosis
q: how is myocarditis treated
what is the prognosis of myocarditis
does myocarditis lead to dilated cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Many cases of myocarditis are not obvious, so management starts with a high index of suspicion. Supportive care is the mainstay, and aggressive hemodynamic stabilization may be needed in a sick patient. As needed, the team uses vasodilators, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, diuretics, antiarrhythmics and anticoagulation.

The outlook varies. Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, but one third later develop dilated cardiomyopathy. That is why myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy are linked: viral myocarditis accounts for 20% of dilated cardiomyopathy.

cards.t: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: what it is and how it is inherited
q: what is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
how is HCM inherited
why is HCM a cause of sudden death in young people
cards.x:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is thickening of the left ventricular muscle that is not explained by a cause such as hypertension, aortic valve disease or an infiltrative or storage disease. It is often asymmetric and can involve any region, most often the interventricular septum (the wall between the two ventricles).

It is mostly inherited, autosomal dominant, meaning one mutated copy from an affected parent is enough. There are at least 1,500 mutations, in genes for sarcomere proteins (the proteins that make muscle contract). It affects 1 in 500 people, males more than females.

It carries a high incidence of sudden death. It is the leading cause of sudden death in preadolescent and adolescent children, with extreme exertion linked to those deaths.

cards.t: Obstructive vs nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is systolic anterior motion
what is the difference between obstructive and nonobstructive HCM
why does HCM cause diastolic dysfunction
cards.x:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy comes in two types, depending on whether the thick muscle blocks blood flow out of the heart.

Without obstruction, the problem is diastolic dysfunction. The thick muscle resists filling (reduced compliance) and raises the pressure at the end of filling in the left ventricle.

With obstruction (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy), the thickened septum narrows the subaortic outflow tract (the path out of the left ventricle). On top of that comes systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve: fast flow through the narrowed path pulls the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve into the outflow tract, causing mid-systolic obstruction. This is the telltale sign of the obstructive form on echocardiography.

Chest pain (angina) can occur without coronary disease because of the outflow obstruction plus the higher oxygen demand of thick muscle.

cards.t: Presentation of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: dyspnea, syncope, sudden death
q: what are the symptoms of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
why is syncope important in HCM
what rhythm causes sudden death in HCM
cards.x:
Many patients have no symptoms and are found through family screening, a murmur on routine exam or an abnormal electrocardiogram.

- Dyspnea is the common presenting symptom: high filling pressure in the ventricle backs up into the lungs.
- Palpitations from atrial premature beats, atrial fibrillation or flutter, or supraventricular or ventricular tachycardia.
- Angina without coronary artery disease.
- Syncope (very common; low output on exertion or an arrhythmia) and presyncope on standing that is relieved by lying down. Both identify patients at high risk of sudden death, and the work-up is urgent. Think of a young athlete who simply passes out.
- Sudden cardiac death, highest in preadolescents and adolescents and related to extreme exertion. Over 80% of cases are ventricular fibrillation.

cards.t: Exam findings and murmurs in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is pulsus bisferiens
where is the HCM murmur heard and where does it radiate
what murmurs are heard in HCM
cards.x:
Blood pressure and heart rate are usually normal. The classic pulse is pulsus bisferiens, Latin for "strike twice": a double systolic peak that matches the outflow obstruction. The apical impulse is forceful and sustained, maybe displaced, and there is a fourth heart sound from the noncompliant (stiff) ventricle.

There are two murmurs.
- The outflow murmur is crescendo-decrescendo and systolic, best heard at the left sternal border in the 3rd or 4th intercostal space. It radiates to the suprasternal notch but not to the carotids or neck.
- The mitral regurgitation murmur, caused by systolic anterior motion, is holosystolic at the apex and radiates to the axilla.

cards.t: How maneuvers change the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy murmur
q: what makes the HCM murmur louder
what makes the HCM murmur softer
does breathing change the HCM murmur
cards.x:
The rule is simple. Anything that puts more blood in the left ventricle softens the murmur. Anything that puts less blood in makes it louder. That is because the amount of blood in the ventricle changes how much the outflow is blocked.

- Rapid squatting and passive leg raising increase preload (the filling volume): the murmur gets softer.
- Handgrip increases afterload (the resistance the ventricle pumps against): softer.
- Valsalva and standing reduce preload: louder.
- Amyl nitrite reduces afterload: louder.
- Inspiration and expiration: no effect.

So standing and Valsalva shrink the filling of the ventricle. That makes the narrowed outflow tighter and the murmur louder. Squatting fills the ventricle and opens things up.

cards.t: Diagnosing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
q: what is the test of choice for HCM
what wall thickness diagnoses HCM
is catheterization needed for HCM
cards.x:
There is no specific blood test. Routine labs only look for things that make it worse, such as anemia, thyroid disease or kidney and liver problems.

Echocardiography is the typical test of choice. The diagnosis is confirmed by unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the left ventricle. Classic findings:
- Asymmetric septal hypertrophy and a small cavity.
- A normal ejection fraction (above 75% late, as the small ventricle nearly empties).
- Mitral regurgitation, systolic anterior motion and left atrial enlargement.

Other tests:
- Electrocardiogram: hypertrophy, atrial enlargement, conduction abnormalities, prominent Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads, left axis deviation.
- Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging when the echocardiogram is questionable, and exercise echocardiography.
- An ambulatory electrocardiogram for 24 to 48 hours assesses the risk of dangerous arrhythmias and sudden death.
- Catheterization is not needed for diagnosis, only before a pacemaker or surgery. Genetic testing is available but does not change treatment.

The differential includes aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, hypertensive heart disease, athletic heart and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

cards.t: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: drugs to use and drugs to avoid
q: what is the first-line drug for obstructive HCM
why avoid nitrates in HCM
what drugs worsen HCM
cards.x:
For outflow obstruction, a beta blocker (for example metoprolol) is the initial medication. The alternative is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem).

The drugs to avoid follow from the mechanism. Drugs that lower preload or afterload, such as nitrates, make the obstruction worse, because an emptier ventricle narrows the outflow tract more. Diuretics are used only with caution to avoid dehydration. Positive inotropes (digoxin, epinephrine, norepinephrine) raise contractility, ischemia risk and arrhythmias, so they are also avoided.

To prevent sudden death, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is used in high-risk patients. Disopyramide can add relief of outflow obstruction. Amiodarone helps control arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation. For atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke. Amiodarone and radiofrequency ablation are also options.

cards.t: Myectomy and alcohol septal ablation
q: what is a septal myectomy
how does alcohol septal ablation work
when is surgery needed in HCM
cards.x:
When medication does not control obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the thick septum can be reduced in two ways.

- Surgical septal myectomy excises part of the septal muscle that is causing the obstruction. The mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion may resolve with the myectomy alone.
- Alcohol septal ablation injects alcohol down the first septal branch of the left anterior descending artery. It creates a therapeutic infarct (a controlled heart attack) of the upper septum, and it takes months for the septum to thin.

If the disease is unresponsive to therapy, transplant is an option.

Patient advice is to stay well hydrated and avoid excess alcohol. Activity advice is individualized. Regular mild to moderate exercise is encouraged. Strenuous or competitive sports need a shared decision with a specialist center. Classic teaching limited patients to mild to moderate, noncompetitive recreational activity. With the obstructive form, it advised no strenuous activity until the work-up is done, because of the risk of dangerous ventricular rhythms and death.

In adolescents, the strategies are genetic screening and activity restriction for high-risk individuals. That is because sudden death is highest in preadolescents and adolescents and is related to extreme exertion.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: what it is
q: what is restrictive cardiomyopathy
why does restrictive cardiomyopathy cause right heart failure
why does it cause heart block
cards.x:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the rarest cardiomyopathy. The problem is impaired diastolic filling with a reasonably preserved chamber size. The walls are normal or slightly thickened, so the heart is 'stiff, but not necessarily thickened.'

The chain: stiff walls, poor filling, then reduced output because the filling volume is reduced. The ejection fraction is preserved until late and systolic function is usually normal. Both atria enlarge, atrial fibrillation is common, and right heart failure is often more prominent. Fibrosis (scarring) of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can cause heart block.

It has the poorest prognosis of all the heart muscle diseases.

cards.t: Causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloidosis and others)
q: what is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy
what causes a stiff heart
which treatments can cause restrictive cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Restrictive cardiomyopathy has several causes to place:

- Idiopathic (no cause found).
- Infiltrative: amyloidosis, the most common in the United States.
- Storage: hemochromatosis, which is iron deposits.
- Genetic, which is less common than in other cardiomyopathies.
- Inflammatory: cardiac sarcoidosis (granulomas).
- Treatment-related: mediastinal radiation and chemotherapy, where inflammation leads to fibrosis (scarring) and then restriction.

Patients often present late, with pronounced symptoms, so ask about prior radiation, chemotherapy or a systemic disease.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: symptoms, exam and Kussmaul sign
q: what is Kussmaul sign
how does restrictive cardiomyopathy present
why is right-sided failure more prominent
cards.x:
It often presents late, with pronounced symptoms. Right-sided failure features: abdominal pain from an enlarged liver, swelling of both feet, ascites. Also progressive exercise intolerance and dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, palpitations from atrial fibrillation (with a risk of atrial clots), fatigue and syncope.

On exam, the patient is more comfortable sitting, jugular venous pressure is elevated, and the heart sounds are normal but perhaps distant. A fourth heart sound is heard if there is no regurgitation. There may be rales, an enlarged congested liver, hepatojugular reflux and ascites.

Kussmaul sign may be present: a paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration, caused by resistance to right ventricular filling. It is also common in constrictive pericarditis, so it does not separate the two.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy vs constrictive pericarditis
q: how do you tell restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis
why can't echocardiography tell them apart
what test separates restrictive from constrictive
cards.x:
Constrictive pericarditis is the look-alike that must be differentiated from restrictive cardiomyopathy. Both leave a heart that cannot fill properly. Both can show Kussmaul sign. In restrictive cardiomyopathy the problem is the heart muscle. In constrictive pericarditis it is the pericardium (the sac around the heart). The cause, treatment and outcome are very different.

The echocardiogram is not definitive on its own, because the two look alike. In restrictive cardiomyopathy it shows a preserved ejection fraction (which may fall late) and marked atrial enlargement. It also shows near-normal ventricular function and cavity size, normal or thick walls, and abnormal diastolic function.

Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging helps separate them. A thickened pericardium points to constrictive pericarditis, though constriction can occur with a normal-thickness pericardium. If imaging and genetic testing are negative, or tissue would change management, an endomyocardial biopsy can be done. Catheterization gives ventricular pressure tracings.

cards.t: Restrictive cardiomyopathy: electrocardiogram, chest X-ray and treatment
q: what does the electrocardiogram show in amyloid heart disease
how do you treat restrictive cardiomyopathy
why be careful with diuretics in restrictive cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
The electrocardiogram depends on the stage and cause. In amyloidosis it shows low QRS (the main spike) voltage, meaning small tracings. Atrial fibrillation and bundle branch blocks are common. The chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart from atrial enlargement, plus congestion and effusions.

Treatment is to treat the underlying disorder, then manage the heart:
- Diuretics for pulmonary and systemic congestion, but with caution. Stiff ventricles depend on preload to keep up their output, and diuretics lower it.
- Beta blockers, and verapamil or diltiazem, are sometimes tried to lengthen filling time and improve relaxation. They are used cautiously because these stiff hearts depend on a fast heart rate to keep output up. Verapamil and diltiazem are avoided in cardiac amyloidosis.
- Anticoagulation to prevent embolism from atrial clots.
- A permanent pacemaker for conduction disease.
- Cardiac transplantation.

The prognosis is the poorest of all the heart muscle diseases.

cards.t: Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: what it is
q: what is Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
why is it called broken heart syndrome
who gets Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, or 'broken heart syndrome,' is temporary weakness of part of the left ventricle's squeeze (transient regional systolic dysfunction). It mimics acute coronary syndrome, yet the coronary arteries show no angiographic disease and there is no acute plaque rupture. The cause is unknown. Takotsubo is Japanese for an octopus trap, a round-bottomed, narrow-necked pot.

About 90% of patients are postmenopausal women. The trigger is a significant emotional or physical stressor: the death of a loved one, bad financial news, a natural disaster, a new diagnosis, surgery, withdrawal from illicit drugs or near drowning. These patients tend to have low or no cardiac risk factors.

The classic abnormality is hypokinesis or akinesis (weak or absent movement) of the mid and apical segments of the left ventricle.

cards.t: Takotsubo: how it looks like a heart attack, tests and management
q: how do you diagnose Takotsubo
how is Takotsubo treated
what is the prognosis of Takotsubo
cards.x:
Chest pain and shortness of breath are the most common symptoms, and there can be palpitations, nausea, vomiting and syncope. The exam is nonspecific. The patient may look like acute coronary syndrome or acute heart failure: anxious and sweaty, with fast or slow rhythm problems.

The tests also look like a heart attack: troponin I and T are usually elevated, B-type natriuretic peptide is frequently elevated, and the electrocardiogram shows ST (a segment of the tracing) elevation and T-wave inversion. The echocardiogram shows hypokinesis or akinesis of the mid and apical segments. Cardiac catheterization confirms the diagnosis, most often showing normal coronary arteries.

Because it mimics a heart attack and there are no reliable early differences, follow the acute coronary syndrome protocols and admit to cardiology. Supportive care is empiric: beta blockers are commonly used but have not been proven to help, anticoagulation if there is a clot in the left ventricle, and diuretics if there is heart failure.

Most patients recover completely.

cards.t: Cardiomyopathy care for adolescents, adults and the elderly
q: how does cardiomyopathy care differ by age
what is done for adolescents with HCM
what is the goal of care in elderly cardiomyopathy
cards.x:
What you emphasize changes with the age group.

- Adolescents: genetic screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and activity restriction for high-risk individuals. This is the age at which hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of sudden death.
- Adults: guideline-directed medical therapy (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, beta blockers, angiotensin receptor blockers, diuretics), devices (an implantable defibrillator, a biventricular pacemaker) and lifestyle measures (sodium restriction, alcohol cessation). In advanced disease, consider an assist device or transplant.
- Elderly: therapy tailored to other illnesses and frailty, cautious use of diuretics and vasodilators, and a focus on symptom control and quality of life, with palliative care discussions in advanced stages.

cards.t: Cardiac rehabilitation and palliative care in cardiomyopathy
q: what does cardiac rehabilitation involve
what is palliative care in cardiomyopathy
when is hospice referral appropriate
cards.x:
Two supports sit alongside medical treatment.

Cardiac rehabilitation programs improve exercise tolerance and quality of life. They include education on taking medicines, nutrition and monitoring symptoms, and psychological support for living with a chronic illness. Home-based rehabilitation suits elderly or mobility-limited patients.

Palliative care does not focus on curing. It focuses on making the patient comfortable and letting them enjoy life. It covers symptom management (shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling), advance care planning and goals-of-care discussions, and support for caregivers and family. In end-stage cardiomyopathy it includes referral to hospice.
